newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Prague seeks talks in Czechoslovak debt dispute. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Prague seeks talks in Czechoslovak debt dispute. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]

text.p: The Czech cabinet repeated on Wednesday its call for more talks on the division of property with Slovakia, an unresolved issue dating from the 1992 break up of the Czechoslovak federation.

Earlier this week, Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar was quoted as saying that as of Tuesday, Slovakia would wipe about 24 billion crowns ($740 million) worth of debt to the Czech Republic carried over from the split of the former Czechoslovak central bank.

But Czech Deputy Prime Minister Jiri Skalicky said on Wednesday that his government's position to discuss property issues only after the Slovak government recognises the debt to the Czech Republic was unchanged (corrects by clarifying the Czech government's condition for talks). "This condition (for talks) certainly was not cancelled," he told a news conference after a regular cabinet meeting.

However, Skalicky added that the cabinet had agreed to shuffle members in its part of the bilateral property commission and would consider a new initiative in August aimed at overcoming deadlock in the talks on the split of Czechoslovak property.
Skalicky did not give any further details, saying the cabinet did not discuss details of the controversial issues.
Skalicky's comments followed statements by Meciar who said his cabinet would erase the 24 billion crown item, which Slovakia has never officially recognised, from the books of the central bank.
The Slovak central bank has refused to comment on the issue. Some analysts have said Meciar was only re-stating his earlier position for political reasons.
The Czechoslovak federation ceased to exist on January 1, 1993, after the two federation partners failed to find an agreement on federal and local governments.

Despite a smooth split known as the "Velvet Divorce", a number of property claims remained unresolved, including Slovakia's demand for a part of Czechoslovak gold reserves, the national airline CSA, and an ocean-going merchant fleet.
The two governments also hold stakes in each others' main commercial bank.
